title: The Set Up

jokes.text: Tom inspects his suit and says 'Brooks Brothers. Bought it right off the mannequin.'
jokes.setup: Ann mentions her friend Justin and calls him 'the greatest guy ever,' prompting Tom to ask 'But does he dress this well?'
jokes.punchline: Tom reveals he literally bought his suit off a store mannequin, treating this as an impressive flex rather than the eccentric admission it is.
jokes.explanation: Classic Tom Haverford character comedy — his vanity and fashion obsession are so deep that buying a suit off a mannequin is presented as a brag. The economy is excellent: the line is short and the punchline lands cleanly. High character integration because only Tom would say this.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Justin? Please. I don't know who that is. But let me tell you who I do know - Tom Haverford, fashion icon. You see this outfit? I didn't just buy these clothes, I bought the entire mannequin display from the store. That's right, I walked in, saw those mannequins looking fresh, and I said, 'I want that.' So now I have seven mannequins at home wearing the exact same thing I'm wearing right now.

jokes.text: Ron in talking head: 'I've been getting a lot of visitors recently, thanks to a stupid and worthless new push to make government officials more accessible to the public.'
jokes.setup: Ron is meant to be describing a new government initiative.
jokes.punchline: He describes public accessibility — an objectively positive civic goal — as 'stupid and worthless,' completely sincerely.
jokes.explanation: This is top-tier Ron Swanson character comedy. His libertarian anti-government philosophy expressed with complete deadpan sincerity — calling a good-faith civic initiative 'stupid and worthless' — is exactly who Ron is. High character integration: no other character on any show could deliver this line. The structure is perfect: the setup sounds neutral, then the punchline recontextualizes it as Ron's worldview. Earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm getting visitors because the Parks Department is a public agency, which means the public has access to it. It's the very thing I've spent my career fighting against.

jokes.text: Citizen complains to Ron: 'There is a disturbing lack of benches in Ramsett Park! I want to sit more!'
jokes.setup: Ron is being subjected to public complaints as part of the accessibility initiative.
jokes.punchline: The citizen's complaint is hilariously petty — 'I want to sit more' — delivered with outrage.
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is the absurd smallness of the complaint vs. the citizen's evident outrage. Works as a quick laugh but isn't deeply crafted — it's a one-note joke about petty government complaints.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: This is a bowl I made. I know it's lopsided and kind of ugly, but I'm really proud of it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: It is lopsided and ugly.

jokes.text: Citizen hands Ron a piece of pottery and says: 'I made this in one of your pottery classes. It's terrible.'
jokes.setup: Another citizen comes to Ron with a complaint/comment as part of the public accessibility initiative.
jokes.punchline: The citizen volunteers their own harsh self-assessment of their pottery — 'It's terrible' — with complete matter-of-factness, making the act of showing it even more baffling.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully absurd moment — the citizen's self-awareness makes it funnier than if they'd praised it. The economy is superb: four words ('It's terrible.') deliver the punchline. The visual element (holding up a bad pot) adds to the laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have to deal with the public. This is the worst nightmare of my life. I would rather sit in a room full of baby eagles, which is ironic because I love eagles.

jokes.text: Ron, alone in talking head after a parade of citizens: 'This is my hell.'
jokes.setup: Ron has been subjected to a stream of public visitors making petty complaints.
jokes.punchline: He summarizes the entire experience in three words with complete, bone-dry sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum impact. 'This is my hell' is the perfect Ron Swanson line — economical to the point of poetry, entirely in character, and landing as a payoff to the escalating parade of citizens. High quotability because it's so clean and adaptable. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor: sharp, unexpected in its bluntness, and perfectly delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Cafeteria Worker
dialogue.line: No lettuce, no tomatoes, no cucumbers, no dressing, no taste.

jokes.text: The cafeteria sandwich named 'The Leslie Knope': salami on pumpernickel with olive juice and extra iceberg.
jokes.setup: Ann notes she can't believe the cafeteria named a sandwich after Leslie, who is touched.
jokes.punchline: The sandwich ingredients are revealed — a deeply unappealing combination — and Leslie's only regret is that she doesn't like it.
jokes.explanation: Two-layer joke: the honor of having a sandwich named after you, undercut by the revolting ingredients, further undercut by Leslie's lament that she doesn't like it. Strong character integration — Leslie's earnest civic pride and her odd tastes are both encapsulated here.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The combination sounds absolutely disgusting

jokes.text: Leslie says she asked the police department if she could have a photo of Dave and when they said no, 'so I stole it.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is talking about missing Dave and sharing a sweet photo of them together.
jokes.punchline: The casual admission that she stole official police property, delivered without any sense of wrongdoing.
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie character comedy — her lawbreaking is entirely in service of her sentiment, and she's completely guileless about it. The structure is clean: sweet setup (trying to get a photo of her ex), absurd escalation (they said no), deadpan punchline (so I stole it). Economy is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I created the Knope sandwich. It's got turkey, avocado, sprouts, and a very special sauce.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Everyone loves it. It's my signature sandwich.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Honestly? I hate it. I don't even like my own sandwich.

jokes.text: April, on why she broke up with Andy: 'Although that's pretty much why I broke up with Andy. He lived way too close to me.'
jokes.setup: April is sympathizing about long-distance relationships ending, noting it's hard to end a relationship because of distance.
jokes.punchline: She reveals she broke up with Andy for the opposite reason — he lived too close to her — completely inverting the sentiment.
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection and character comedy. The setup is a sympathetic statement about distance ending relationships; April inverts it perfectly. 'He lived way too close to me' is both a perfect April line (misanthropic, withholding) and a great structural reversal. High quotability. This is in the range of the 8.0 anchor — sharp, economical, character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need that photo of you. It's perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: No, Leslie. That's my official police photo.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, but I need it for my office. It'll only take a second to scan.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Absolutely not.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Fine. Well, I guess I'll just have to steal it from your desk when you're not looking.

jokes.text: April arrives late and Jerry confronts her: 'Wow, 12:15! You're early today.' / 'April, there's no paper in the printer.' / 'So?' / 'So that's the one thing you do.'
jokes.setup: April is a spectacularly indifferent intern who barely does any work.
jokes.punchline: 12:15 being 'early' for April, and the revelation that her entire job description is one task she still neglects.
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy that efficiently establishes April's work ethic (or lack thereof). The exchange is quick and well-structured. Not groundbreaking but competently executed.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, long-distance relationships are really hard.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: But you know what my problem was? Andy lived too close. He was always around. I couldn't get any alone time.

jokes.text: April announces on intercom: 'Attention. April stop doing that.' Then immediately: 'Jerry told me to, so it's super crucial.'
jokes.setup: Ron is trying to get April's attention; she's been making an announcement over the intercom.
jokes.punchline: April uses the intercom to address herself, then deflects responsibility to Jerry while calling it 'super crucial' — transparently insincere.
jokes.explanation: Enjoyable April laziness gag. Announcing her own name over the intercom is a good absurdist beat, and blaming Jerry is perfectly in character. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: There's no paper in the printer.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Okay.

jokes.text: Ron in talking head: 'But now, I need the taxpayers' money to save me from the taxpayers.'
jokes.setup: Ron explains he's saved the city $150,000 by refusing to hire an assistant for eight years.
jokes.punchline: The chiastic reversal — using taxpayer money to hide from taxpayers — is both a great line and a perfect encapsulation of Ron's libertarian-but-still-employed paradox.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The rhetorical structure (taxpayers' money / save me from the taxpayers) is elegant and witty, and it perfectly captures Ron's ideological contradiction: a man who hates government working in government, now using public funds to avoid the public. Economy is near-perfect. High quotability. Comparable to or slightly above the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no idea what you're talking about. I don't waste government money. I respect the taxpayers.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you once spent $50,000 on a hunting trip that you said was a 'government resource.'

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That was a necessary expenditure. And besides, I need more government funding so I can avoid dealing with the public.

jokes.text: Ron's job posting looks like 'an ad for nothing' and he says 'Please be careful with it, it's my only copy.'
jokes.setup: Ron gives Tom a job posting to put up at a college so he can find an assistant.
jokes.punchline: Tom points out it looks like an ad for nothing; Ron's response reveals he only made one copy, emphasizing his contempt for the whole enterprise.
jokes.explanation: A solid visual gag with a good secondary payoff ('it's my only copy'). The combination of Ron's minimalist approach to hiring and the absurd scarcity of one copy is on-brand. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This job posting is so vague. It could mean anything. Are you looking for someone to organize your files, or murder someone and make it look like an accident?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Well, the files are a disaster.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So... murder?

jokes.text: Leslie asks Justin if his specialty is 'locking up the bad guys or keeping them on the streets?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is warming up to Justin and asks about his legal specialty.
jokes.punchline: Her two options — locking up bad guys OR keeping them on the streets — are both criminal law and both slightly absurd framings, suggesting she has no idea what lawyers actually do.
jokes.explanation: Good Leslie naivety joke — she's framing law as a binary good-vs-evil question that misses how civil litigation works. The 'keeping them on the streets' option is the funnier of the two. Solid character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: April, I need you to handle this job posting. But whatever you do, do not let it fall into the wrong hands.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's a job posting.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Exactly. Which is why the government will stop at nothing to get it. They'll use it to track our hiring patterns, predict our staffing needs, anticipate our moves. It's a roadmap to our vulnerabilities.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ron, it's literally just a form.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's what they want you to think. Guard it with your life.

jokes.text: Justin explains he's suing 'Fire in a Can' — an aerosol can with an igniter invented to warm up baby bottles that will 'literally burn your hand clean off.'
jokes.setup: Justin says he has a crazy case; Leslie says she loves the Fire in a Can commercials.
jokes.punchline: The product is revealed to be essentially a blowtorch invented for baby bottles — an escalating series of absurd details.
jokes.explanation: The comedy escalates nicely: fun product → burn your hand off → aerosol igniter → invented for baby bottles. Each detail is more absurd than the last. Works well as world-building humor.

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: Any friend of Ann's...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: ...is a friend of mine! That's going to be my new motto. I'm going to have it embroidered on a throw pillow.

jokes.text: Tom enters the conference room and immediately compliments Justin: 'You are wearing the hell out of that suit, sir. Banana, two-button.'
jokes.setup: Leslie introduces Tom to Justin in the conference room.
jokes.punchline: Tom's first words to a stranger are a fashion analysis — 'Banana, two-button' — delivered with professional authority, treating suit identification as the most important thing about a person.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Tom Haverford moment — he meets a new person and immediately evaluates their suit with expert-level shorthand. The detail 'Banana, two-button' reads as authentic fashion knowledge, which makes it funnier. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So what kind of law do you practice?

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: Corporate law, mostly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh. So you're not a criminal lawyer?

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's too bad. I feel like that's the only kind of lawyer.

jokes.text: Intern confessional: 'I come in, like, two hours late because I had to finish watching Swimfan because it was on, and everyone, like, jumped down my throat.'
jokes.setup: The intern is doing a talking-head confessional, apparently complaining about the workplace.
jokes.punchline: The reason for being two hours late is finishing the 2002 thriller Swimfan because it was on TV — completely unashamed and oblivious.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Swimfan is key — it's not a great movie, it's a random cable movie, and the intern treats it as a valid excuse. The cluelessness is the joke. Solid laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: A blowtorch with an innocent intended purpose? That's just a blowtorch.

jokes.text: Andy improvises a song: 'I have been writing a lot of songs about shining shoes lately. I tend to write about what I'm doing. Talking about writing about what I'm doing. Now I'm singing about talking about writing about what I'm doing.'
jokes.setup: Ann suggests Andy sell his band's CDs at the shoe-shine stand.
jokes.punchline: Andy begins improvising a meta-recursive song that keeps adding layers ('talking about writing about what I'm doing'), each iteration making it more absurd.
jokes.explanation: A standout moment. Andy's meta-recursive song is genuinely inventive — it escalates in real time, each new line describing the act of singing the previous line. It's self-referential comedy that also works as character comedy (Andy is guileless enough to think this is deep). The structure is elegant: each escalation adds exactly one layer. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor and above.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Hold up. Is that a Tom Ford suit?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Because the stitching on the lapels, the way the fabric drapes, the cut of the jacket—that's Tom Ford. I would know Tom Ford anywhere. I am basically Tom Ford.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Those are Allen Edmonds shoes. Italian leather, hand-stitched. Those are at least $600.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And that pocket square—that's a Hermès. You've got good taste, my friend. Real good taste.

jokes.text: Leslie does dating math and concludes she won't be over Dave for 500 years.
jokes.setup: Leslie explains her pattern: one night with Mark, then hung up for six years; three months with Dave; therefore if she continues the pattern...
jokes.punchline: The calculation yields '500 years' — an absurd but internally logical result that Leslie apparently accepts.
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy with good structural payoff. The setup (establishing the pattern) earns the punchline. The pause before '500 years' (inferred from the timestamp gap) adds comedic timing. Leslie's earnest pseudo-mathematical approach to romance is perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Intern/Student
dialogue.line: My supervisor said I was late again today. I told him it wasn't my fault.

dialogue.speaker: Intern/Student
dialogue.line: I said, 'Sir, I was stuck in traffic behind a parade of tiny horses. What was I supposed to do?'

jokes.text: Leslie's ideal man: 'He has the brains of George Clooney in the body of Joe Biden.'
jokes.setup: Ann asks Leslie what her ideal man is.
jokes.punchline: Leslie inverts the usual formulation (brains of X, body of Y) by putting the intellectual celebrity in the 'brains' slot and the politician in the 'body' slot — suggesting she finds Joe Biden physically attractive.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most quotable lines. The inversion is the joke: you'd expect 'brains of Biden, body of Clooney,' but Leslie flips it — she's attracted to Biden's physical form and wants Clooney's brains. It's deeply character-specific (Leslie's love of government and civic figures), structurally tight, and genuinely surprising. High quotability. Firmly in 8+ territory.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So I was writing this song, right? And I thought, 'What rhymes with orange?' Nothing rhymes with orange. So I wrote a song that's just me saying 'orange' over and over for four minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I call it 'Orange.'

jokes.text: Ann's reaction: 'Interesting. That's uh... weird.'
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers her Joe Biden/George Clooney ideal man description.
jokes.punchline: Ann's stumbling, ultimately settling on 'weird' is the straight-man reaction that validates the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: A necessary and well-timed reaction beat that extends the laugh from joke 18. Ann's 'weird' lands because of the buildup, but on its own it's a straight-man moment, not a fully crafted joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm writing a song about writing a song about writing a song.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So the first verse is about how I'm writing a song, the second verse is about how I'm writing a song about writing a song, and then the third verse is about how I'm writing a song about writing a song about writing a song.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's very meta. Very deep.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Andy, that's just... that's the same thing three times.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Exactly! See, you get it!

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I don't want to date a twin, 'cause I've been tricked before.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving Ann rules for who to set her up with.
jokes.punchline: The rule is 'no twins' — but the real joke is 'cause I've been tricked before,' implying a whole backstory of twin-related romantic deception.
jokes.explanation: A gem. The rule itself is unexpected, but 'because I've been tricked before' is what elevates it — it implies a rich, unexplained history and trusts the audience to fill in the gap. No exposition, no follow-up. The economy is near-perfect. Highly quotable and rewatch-worthy. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So what's your ideal man?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, he has to be intelligent, ambitious, and passionate about public service. He should care deeply about the environment and social justice. Ideally, he'd be a Democrat, but I could compromise for a really progressive Independent. He needs to understand that my career will always come first, and he has to be okay with that. Also, he should be tall, but not too tall—I don't want to crane my neck. He needs to appreciate breakfast foods as much as I do.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's very specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know what I want, Ann. I'm not going to settle for some Republican who thinks climate change is a hoax.

jokes.text: Tom calls Ron 'Ron Solo.'
jokes.setup: Tom approaches Ron's office.
jokes.punchline: He greets Ron with 'Ron Solo' — a Star Wars reference combining Ron's name with Han Solo, appropriate given Ron's lone-wolf, self-sufficient personality.
jokes.explanation: Quick nickname gag that works on two levels (Tom's pop culture fluency, Ron's rugged independence). Not deeply crafted but fun and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So you're looking for a man who's six foot three, has the torso of an Olympian, the mind of a Renaissance man, and the soul of a golden retriever?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's not a man. That's a Pinterest board.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Yeah, my friends know that I have a strict no-call policy. Now get out there and find me an assistant.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks how Ron knows a person was a member of the public rather than a friend.
jokes.punchline: Ron has a 'strict no-call policy' with his friends — meaning he doesn't call or receive calls from anyone — and states it as though it's perfectly normal.
jokes.explanation: Strong Ron character moment — the 'no-call policy' with friends deepens his anti-social mythology. Clean delivery and good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay Ann, here are the dating rules. Rule one: never date a guy who has a pet snake. Rule two: never date a guy who collects anything. Rule three: never date a guy who uses the word 'utilize' instead of 'use.'

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Why are you telling me all this?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because I've made every single one of these mistakes. I dated a guy who had all three. He had a pet snake named Utilize that he kept in a collection of aquariums.

jokes.text: Ann's response to blood on scrubs: 'Oh, damn, now I have to go back.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if the blood on Ann's scrubs is 'his blood.'
jokes.punchline: Ann confirms it by saying she has to go back, treating it as a minor inconvenience, not a medical emergency — dark implication played completely straight.
jokes.explanation: The dark comedy is in the casualness — Ann treats a bleeding patient as an errand. Economy is excellent. Works as a secondary beat to joke 23.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yo, Darth Swanson!

jokes.text: Leslie deliberates over identification methods for the blind date: red rose, giant red hat, then 'I don't have one of those.' Ann: 'I will just tell him what you look like.'
jokes.setup: Leslie needs a way for her date to identify her at the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: After escalating to 'a giant red hat' (which she doesn't own), Ann's simple solution — just describing Leslie — deflates the whole overthought situation.
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy. Leslie overcomplicates the obvious, Ann provides the simple answer. Predictable structure but warm and relatable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: How did you know it was a public call and not a friend?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Because a friend wouldn't call me. I have a rule: if you're my friend, you don't contact me.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Friendship is two people using each other to get what they want and refusing to be honest about it. But I'm done with that. I'm going off the grid.

jokes.text: Ann is visibly watching from outside the restaurant as Leslie's date goes well, and says 'Well done, Ann.' Chris hears: 'I actually heard that.'
jokes.setup: Ann is apparently watching the date from somewhere nearby and congratulates herself out loud.
jokes.punchline: Chris, who is inside with Leslie, can hear Ann — breaking the illusion that Ann was discreetly observing.
jokes.explanation: A nice visual/spatial gag — Ann is close enough for Chris to hear, undermining her discreet observation. The reveal is quick and clean.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my god, is that blood?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I work at a hospital, of course it's blood.

jokes.text: Chris immediately says 'Boo! Indiana Hoosiers!' when Leslie cheers 'Go Badgers!'
jokes.setup: Chris reveals he went to Wisconsin; Leslie, an Indiana grad, cheers for Wisconsin out of politeness.
jokes.punchline: Chris immediately fires back 'Boo! Indiana Hoosiers!' — transforming the polite social exchange into a sports rivalry.
jokes.explanation: Functional but not especially crafted. The sports rivalry joke is relatable but generic. Chris's immediate 'boo' is a good beat that sets up his slightly oblivious character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, this setup is absolutely perfect. You've really outdone yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Thank you, Leslie!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I couldn't help but overhear. Ann, that's excellent work. Really excellent.

jokes.text: Chris corrects Leslie that her job isn't amusement parks but 'regular parks. Like swings and slides and stuff.' Then says 'Strike two.'
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions Ann told Chris she's in charge of amusement parks.
jokes.punchline: She clarifies it's just regular parks; Chris calls this 'Strike two,' establishing a running tally of disappointments on the date.
jokes.explanation: Sets up the escalating failure of the date. 'Strike two' works because it implies a 'strike one' we may not have seen (presumably the college teams), giving the date a scorecard structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: So... do you come here often?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I read that's what people say on dates. I don't actually know if you come here often. That would be weird if I already knew that.

jokes.text: Chris says: 'You know, isn't it funny how these setups are always just so awkward?' making the date immediately awkward.
jokes.setup: The date is going acceptably; Chris tries to make a relatable observation.
jokes.punchline: His comment about setups being awkward immediately creates the awkwardness he described, in real time.
jokes.explanation: Self-fulfilling prophecy comedy — a classic cringe structure. Chris naming the awkwardness creates it, and the subsequent exchange ('Did I just make it awkward?' / 'No.' / 'Well, yeah, you kind of did.') extends the laugh with a well-timed partial denial.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Leslie, I want to show you something impressive. I've been working on my flexibility.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh really? What are you going to do?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm going to touch my toes without bending my knees.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, go ahead.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Nnnngh... aaahhhhh... OH GOD. Oh no. Oh no no no.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Are you okay?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I think I pulled something. Several somethings. Everything hurts. Why did I do this?

jokes.text: Beat of silence/hesitation, then Leslie admits: 'Well, yeah, you kind of did.' (about Chris making it awkward)
jokes.setup: Chris asks if he made it awkward; Leslie initially says no.
jokes.punchline: After a pause, she admits he kind of did — the honesty landing harder after the polite deflection.
jokes.explanation: The timing is everything here — the pause between 'No' and 'Well, yeah, you kind of did' is the joke. Good reaction beat that extends joke 29.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I learned this trick online.

jokes.text: Chris announces: 'Hey, watch this. I will now extinguish this candle with my bare hand.' Then screams in pain: 'That really hurt!'
jokes.setup: Chris decides to show off by extinguishing a restaurant candle with his bare hand.
jokes.punchline: He immediately burns himself and cries out in pain, admitting 'It looked so much easier on the Internet.'
jokes.explanation: 'It looked so much easier on the Internet' is the key line — it characterizes Chris as the kind of guy who gets his confidence from YouTube and spectacularly fails in public. Good physical comedy beat on a bad date.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Leslie, can I borrow some ice for my hand? I burned it on the stove.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, yes! I would love some ice water right now, thank you so much.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: No, no, I need ice for my burn.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh... I thought you were being really generous and weird.

jokes.text: 'That really hurt!' / 'Are you okay?' / 'Oh God! It looked so much easier on the Internet. God, I gotta borrow some of your ice!'
jokes.setup: Chris has just burned his hand on the candle
jokes.punchline: 'It looked so much easier on the Internet' — his explanation perfectly captures the era's specific brand of amateur overconfidence
jokes.explanation: Strong topper to the candle gag. 'Easier on the Internet' is the episode's most quotable single-joke-topper line and has aged well as a universal truth. The desperation of borrowing Leslie's ice mid-date adds physical comedy dimension.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Justin is like... he's like a human being, but better. He's got all the regular human features, but they're arranged in a way that makes sense. Like, his face is a face, but it's a GOOD face. And when he talks, words come out, but they're the right words in the right order. I've never experienced that before.

jokes.text: Chris screams in pain, shoves his hand in Leslie's water glass to cool the burn. Leslie says: 'Oh no thanks. I'm not thirsty.'
jokes.setup: Chris burns himself and grabs Leslie's ice water to soothe his hand.
jokes.punchline: Leslie responds as though he'd offered her the water to drink, completely missing/ignoring what he's doing with her glass.
jokes.explanation: Excellent deadpan misdirection. Leslie's 'Oh no thanks. I'm not thirsty' is perfectly timed and completely absurd — she either doesn't understand what's happening or is so checked out from the disastrous date that she's auto-piloting polite responses. The economy is nearly perfect. Earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So let me ask you something. If you could have dinner with any person, living or dead, who would it be?

dialogue.speaker: Candidate
dialogue.line: Um... I guess Abraham Lincoln?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wrong. It's me. You should want to have dinner with me. I'm your potential boss.

jokes.text: Tom's job description: 'Just your basic assistant stuff. Taking messages, wake-up calls, bottle service at The Snakehole Lounge, condom runs, covering for me at any legally dicey situations.'
jokes.setup: Tom describes what the assistant position involves.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from mundane tasks to deeply inappropriate ones — 'condom runs' and 'legally dicey situations' — delivered as though they're equally normal.
jokes.explanation: Great escalation joke. The list structure works perfectly — each item is more absurd than the last, culminating in 'legally dicey situations.' The deadpan delivery and the matter-of-fact framing are key. High character integration — only Tom would describe this as 'basic assistant stuff.'

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so you've got two options here. This tie or this tie.

dialogue.speaker: Candidate
dialogue.line: Um, those are the same tie.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, no, no. One is slightly more burgundy. But here's the thing—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You've been thinking about this all wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The correct tie was hidden the whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's this one.

jokes.text: Tom's interview question for assistant candidate: 'I got a nightclub opening to go to. Which tie do I wear?' Candidate picks one. Tom: 'That was a trick question. The answer's this one. I didn't even know that one existed.'
jokes.setup: Tom is interviewing candidates for Ron's assistant position and claims to be interested in 'real world expertise.'
jokes.punchline: His test is a trick tie question where the 'correct' answer is a tie the candidate didn't know existed — making the test literally impossible to pass.
jokes.explanation: Classic Tom Haverford absurdity — conducting a job interview based entirely on fashion. The trick tie is perfect: he presents two options, the candidate picks one, and Tom reveals a secret third tie. The logic is internally consistent for Tom's worldview. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I'm not saying the government is hiding aliens in the basement of the library. I'm just saying nobody's ever shown me the basement, and that's suspicious.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Also, has anyone ever actually seen a platypus in real life? Or is it just a concept they made up to distract us?

jokes.text: Tom to interview candidate: 'I had high hopes when I saw your plumbed V-Neck. But those hopes have been dashed. You can leave.'
jokes.setup: The candidate failed Tom's tie trick question.
jokes.punchline: Tom dismisses the candidate based entirely on fashion criteria, treating 'plumbed V-neck' as a meaningful positive indicator that was then squandered.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the interview joke. Tom's fashion-based hiring criteria being delivered with HR-manager gravity is funny. 'Those hopes have been dashed' is a nice formal phrase applied to fashion disappointment.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: The MRI machine is capable of detecting tumors, lesions, and abnormalities in virtually any part of the body. It can image the brain, the spine, the joints, the organs, soft tissue, blood vessels, and bones. It's also great for detecting things like paperclips, staples, loose change, button collections, those little plastic tabs on bread bags, expired coupons, and basically any metallic or semi-metallic object that might be lodged in or around your body for some reason.

jokes.text: Chris explains MRI work: 'In less than an hour, I know what it is. What's wrong with her?' / 'I don't know.'
jokes.setup: Chris builds up to describing the satisfaction of MRI work — a mother comes in scared, and soon he'll know what's wrong.
jokes.punchline: The dramatic buildup deflates entirely: he doesn't actually know what's wrong with her (he just identifies something in the image; diagnosis is the doctor's job).
jokes.explanation: Good structural misdirection — the theatrical buildup makes the flat 'I don't know' more effective. It also characterizes Chris as someone who doesn't quite understand the limits of his own role, which tracks with his behavior throughout the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Bread is just bread. It doesn't contain anything else. It's just bread.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, that's where you're wrong. Bread is made of bread crumbs, and bread crumbs are just tiny pieces of bread. So technically, bread contains bread, which makes it circular, which makes it fine.

jokes.text: Candidate interview: 'Did you ever see that movie The Matrix?' 'Yeah.' '99% real.'
jokes.setup: Tom is giving the candidate 'real world expertise' questions.
jokes.punchline: Tom reveals he believes The Matrix is 99% real — delivered with complete confidence as though this is relevant insider knowledge.
jokes.explanation: Three words ('99% real') delivering maximum absurdity. The confidence and brevity are what make it — Tom says it as if he's sharing classified information. High economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Leslie, I want you to get a free MRI.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Because I care about you, and I want to make sure you're healthy. Plus, if anything happens to you, my life loses like 40% of its value.

jokes.text: Chris describes MRI capabilities: 'I can look inside this steak or this butter or the potatoes or this candle or this beer or this flower or this bread.'
jokes.setup: Chris is enthusiastically explaining that an MRI can see inside anything.
jokes.punchline: His list of things he could MRI spirals into all the objects on the restaurant table — beer, flowers, bread — in escalating absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Chris's excitement about MRIs is infectious and slightly unhinged. The list escalation works well and characterizes him as someone who's maybe too into his job.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: And we'll tell our grandkids about our weird first date.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, and how you were creepy.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Well, if you look inside this bread, all you're gonna find is more bread.' Chris: 'I don't know. I'd have to do an MRI.'
jokes.setup: Chris says he can look inside anything with an MRI.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's observation (bread contains bread) is obviously true; Chris refusing to commit without an MRI is a perfect character moment.
jokes.explanation: The exchange is tight and funny. Leslie's deadpan logic vs. Chris's professional paranoia ('I'd have to do an MRI') is a great character clash. The follow-up ('Just bread in there.' / 'Yeah but what's inside that bread?') extends it nicely with an additional layer.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You can't smile during an MRI. It disrupts the magnetic field.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not true.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, the thing is, your teeth are made of metal. And metal is magnetic. So if you smile, the magnet sucks all the metal out of your teeth, and then your teeth fall out.

jokes.text: Chris offers Leslie a free MRI scan on their first date. 'Well, I'm offering you a free scan. It usually costs up to $2,000. I'm kind of spoiling you here.'
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions she's never had an MRI.
jokes.punchline: Chris immediately offers her a free MRI as though it's a romantic gesture, framing it as spoiling her.
jokes.explanation: Chris blurring professional and romantic in the most oblivious way. 'I'm kind of spoiling you here' is the key line — he genuinely believes an MRI is a romantic treat. Great cringe comedy setup for the scene that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So here's my strategy. I wait exactly three days before texting back. It shows I'm busy, I'm confident, I don't need her.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Then I send something super casual, like 'yo' or a thumbs up emoji.

jokes.text: Chris, while preparing Leslie for the MRI: 'Frankly, I don't want to invest in someone who only has three months to live.'
jokes.setup: Chris is framing the MRI as a date activity and a health check.
jokes.punchline: His reasoning is that he doesn't want to date someone with a terminal diagnosis — treating Leslie as a potential investment with actuarial risk.
jokes.explanation: Darkly funny — screening a date for terminal illness before investing emotionally. The word 'invest' is perfect: it makes the cruelty feel like rational thinking, which is the joke. Well-crafted dark comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I also cover all of your illegal activities. Nothing? Really? Because I have a list here.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I'm treating this as an adventure. Who knows, maybe someday we'll tell our grandkids about how weird our first date was.' Chris: 'And how creepy their grandfather was.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to put a positive spin on the bizarre date.
jokes.punchline: Chris cheerfully agrees that he's creepy — no defensiveness, just complete self-awareness that doesn't change his behavior at all.
jokes.explanation: Chris's self-aware admission of creepiness without any intention to stop is a good beat. His comfort with his own strangeness is a consistent character note that makes this land.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I charge a finder's fee because I provide a valuable service. As the great philosopher once said, 'If you want results, you gotta pay for results.' That's what Rod Blagojevich taught us.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Try not to smile too much. It'll affect the diagnosis.' Then: 'Sometimes smiling is read as AIDS.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is getting into the MRI machine on their date.
jokes.punchline: Chris warns her smiling could be misread, then reveals the specific misreading: AIDS. The medical implausibility is so extreme it becomes absurdist.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly absurd line. 'Sometimes smiling is read as AIDS' is medically nonsensical but delivered with complete clinical authority, making it a great example of false expertise comedy. The escalation from 'don't smile' to 'AIDS' is perfectly compressed. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: It's like a roast chicken in there. I'm just saying, that's a lot of dark meat.

jokes.text: Chris, preparing Leslie for the MRI: 'Oh, you're not on your period, are you?' Then to her confused look: 'Well, not for this.'
jokes.setup: Chris is running through MRI safety questions with his date.
jokes.punchline: 'Well, not for this' implies the period question is relevant to other things — adding a layer of inappropriateness to an already uncomfortable date.
jokes.explanation: The implication of 'not for this' is the joke — Chris immediately contextualizes a medical question in a deeply inappropriate way. Works as cringe escalation on the date from hell.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Oh, so you didn't set Leslie up with Justin because Leslie's kind? That's the problem with Leslie. She's too nice. She should be more of a jerk like me.

jokes.text: Tom's interview scenario: 'I meet a girl at a bar... I get her number, it's two days later, what do I text her?' Candidate says 'It was nice meeting you.' Tom: 'No, Zack! I wait eight weeks and I text her, "What's cracking?"'
jokes.setup: Tom poses a dating scenario as an interview question.
jokes.punchline: His answer — waiting eight weeks before texting 'What's cracking?' — is a strategy so wrong it circles back to being its own bizarre comedy.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tom joke. Eight weeks is absurdly long, and 'What's cracking?' is the perfectly wrong text to send after eight weeks. The juxtaposition of the long wait with the casual opener is the heart of the joke. The candidate's reasonable answer (nice meeting you) vs. Tom's confident wrongness is a great structural contrast. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: If that had been a real brain shadow, I would have had to donate my body to science, become a medical mystery, possibly inspire a made-for-TV movie, and my legacy would have been 'the guy with the mysterious brain shadow.'

jokes.text: Candidate: 'I'm sorry. What do I get out of this?' Tom: 'Connections. Plus 19 grand a year, minus my 10% headhunters' fee.'
jokes.setup: The candidate pushes back on the absurd job description.
jokes.punchline: Tom's answer includes a salary plus his own self-invented headhunters' fee — meaning he's charging the candidate he's supposedly helping.
jokes.explanation: The hustle within the hustle — Tom charging the person he's placing as if he's a legitimate recruiter — is a good extension of his character's grift tendencies.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Leslie almost being disabled would've been a real tragedy, because she's such a hard worker. I mean, imagine if she lost her legs—she'd have to use a wheelchair, and she'd probably just wheel herself around the office so fast that she'd crash into a wall.

jokes.text: Tom quotes Rod Blagojevich: 'In the immortal words of Rod Blagojevich, "It's a (fucking) valuable thing. You just don't give it away for nothing."'
jokes.setup: Tom is justifying his headhunter fee.
jokes.punchline: He cites the famously corrupt Illinois governor's corruption wiretap quote as inspirational wisdom — treating a criminal scandal as career advice.
jokes.explanation: Tom citing a corruption scandal as 'immortal words' is a great dark comedy beat. The reference is specific enough to be smart (Blagojevich's wiretap quote is well-known) and perfectly applied to Tom's shady headhunting scheme. Good topical wit.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I mean, if Justin and I ever broke up, I guess I could date Mark. Unless he died in some sort of tragic accident or something.

jokes.text: Chris, scanning Leslie's brain: 'Did you ever break your arm? [...] It was, like, three years ago.' Chris: 'I can't believe I turned the machine off for that.'
jokes.setup: Chris has been asking Leslie not to talk during the MRI, then turns off the machine to let her answer a question about a broken arm.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's arm break was only three years ago — presumably recent enough to still show on a scan — and Chris realizes he stopped the MRI for a completely obvious answer.
jokes.explanation: Good procedural absurdity — Chris makes a big deal of turning off a complex medical machine for an answer he could have guessed. His exasperation is funny, and the line about turning off the machine is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm done. And let me tell you something - you're going to regret this. Because I'm a catch. I'm a really good guy. I have a job, I have a car, I floss regularly. So... enjoy being alone forever.

jokes.text: Chris, reading Leslie's MRI: 'You've got a great oven... You got ample room in there. Honestly, if you wanted to, you could go triplets right off the bat, Leslie. You got a big, industrial-sized oven.'
jokes.setup: Chris is reviewing Leslie's MRI results, specifically her reproductive anatomy.
jokes.punchline: He describes her uterus in terms of kitchen appliances — 'great oven,' 'industrial-sized' — with the clinical enthusiasm of someone evaluating a house.
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable cringe comedy. The 'oven' metaphor is used with complete sincerity, and 'industrial-sized' takes it to a new level. 'You could go triplets right off the bat' is the escalating absurdity that makes the scene memorable. Chris means it as a compliment, which is the most uncomfortable part.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So that was... well, that happened.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yeah, it did.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean, the waiter seemed nice at least.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: He did. You know, my son really enjoyed watching the whole thing from the kitchen.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Your... what?

jokes.text: Ann calls Leslie during the MRI: 'Good! We just finished the MRI.' / 'What?'
jokes.setup: Ann checks in on the date, hoping it's going well.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's casual 'we just finished the MRI' lands as a complete non-sequitur to Ann, who has no context for why a first date involves a medical procedure.
jokes.explanation: A good punctuation beat on the date subplot. Ann's 'What?' is the audience surrogate reaction. The comedy of normalization — Leslie treating the MRI as a normal date activity — is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I got an MRI today.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh nice, an MRI. That's like an X-ray, right? Did they find anything cool? Like a tumor shaped like a celebrity?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, Tom. It's magnetic resonance imaging. It's completely safe and non-invasive.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So they just took a picture of your insides? That's sick. Did you at least get copies?

jokes.text: Mark's talking head: 'Leslie is a notoriously cruel and thoughtless person. Why are we talking about this?'
jokes.setup: Mark and Ann are discussing Ann setting Leslie up; Ann says she didn't set Leslie up with Justin.
jokes.punchline: Mark pivots to a mock-serious assessment of Leslie as 'notoriously cruel and thoughtless,' then immediately deflects as though he didn't say anything.
jokes.explanation: The punchline is the reversal — calling Leslie 'notoriously cruel and thoughtless' when she's obviously neither, then immediately abandoning the topic. Works as sarcasm and character deflection.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Usually I'm the one who's all sunshine and optimism, and April's the one who's dark and cynical. But now it's like we've switched places! She's all happy and bright, and I'm just a dark cloud raining on everything. Or like a vampire. A sad vampire. Who doesn't even want to drink blood anymore because what's the point?

jokes.text: Chris sees a shadow on Leslie's MRI, panics, then: 'Oh wait. It's like a smudge or something. We almost wheeled you out of here in a chair.'
jokes.setup: Chris sees something on Leslie's MRI scan and builds genuine concern ('That's weird... I'd have a doctor look at that immediately').
jokes.punchline: It's just a smudge on the machine — and Chris's reaction is 'we almost wheeled you out of here in a chair,' framing an almost-false-alarm as a near-catastrophe.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe escalation — the MRI date goes from uncomfortable to medically terrifying to 'just a smudge.' The payoff ('we almost wheeled you out in a chair') is delivered with characteristic Chris obliviousness about how alarming that would have been.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so I'm putting myself equal with Justin, and we're both way above Mark.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Imagine if you had spent the rest of your life sipping a steak through a straw. That almost happened to you. You were a smudge away.'
jokes.setup: The MRI scare is revealed to be a smudge; Chris tries to frame their shared near-miss as bonding.
jokes.punchline: 'Sipping a steak through a straw' is a vividly absurd image of brain damage — and 'you were a smudge away' frames a non-event as a catastrophe.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest lines. 'Sipping a steak through a straw' is a genuinely original and viscerally funny image of severe brain damage — specific, unexpected, and darkly comic. 'You were a smudge away' makes it worse by suggesting the fake diagnosis was real. High originality, high quotability. Earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm gonna take relationship advice from you. That's a great idea.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Thank God I was here.' Leslie: 'Looks like we make a pretty good team.'
jokes.setup: Chris has just revealed his 'brain shadow' was a smudge on the machine he operates.
jokes.punchline: Chris takes credit for saving Leslie from a problem he essentially created; Leslie, being Leslie, tries to find the positive.
jokes.explanation: Functional beat — Chris's self-congratulation for fixing a problem he caused is classic oblivious character comedy. Leslie's 'pretty good team' is a nice Leslie-optimism touch.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I was really into Justin, you know? Like, really into him. But then you kept talking about him, and talking about him, and I realized... I don't actually like Justin. I like the idea of Justin. The Justin you described. Not the real Justin.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So really, this is your fault for making him sound so good.

jokes.text: Ann, about Justin: '...or you die tragically in a city planning accident and I'll wait a respectful amount of time. I don't know, maybe?'
jokes.setup: Mark confronts Ann about 'saving' Justin for later. Ann denies having a backup plan.
jokes.punchline: Ann admits that if Mark dies in a 'city planning accident' she might pursue Justin after a respectful wait — the specificity of 'city planning accident' and the casual delivery make it.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy. 'City planning accident' is a hilariously specific cause of death for Mark (a city planner), and Ann's breezy 'I don't know, maybe?' after planning her boyfriend's replacement is deliciously callous. The specificity of the profession-based death is what makes this line outstanding. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because he's not my type. He's not smart, he's not funny, and frankly, Tom, his penis is small.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa! Leslie!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? You're the one who said 'Why don't you date Justin?' I'm just being honest.

jokes.text: Leslie breaks up with Chris: 'I think this is gonna be our last date.' Chris: 'I get it. Get your MRI and get out, huh?' Then: 'This was your idea.' Chris: 'Clever lady.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Chris she doesn't want to see him again.
jokes.punchline: Chris frames the date as an MRI transaction that Leslie manipulated — 'get your MRI and get out' — and when she correctly points out it was his idea, he calls her 'Clever lady,' completely misreading the situation.
jokes.explanation: Good exit beat for Chris's character. His inability to accurately read the situation — calling Leslie 'clever' for a scheme she didn't execute — is perfectly in character and ends his arc on a funny note.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yeah, so I heard you're looking for someone to work here. I'm very qualified. I've had like 300 jobs.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's not a qualification.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Well, I'm also very good with the ladies. Your intern April? I'd like to take her out sometime.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Why not? She's smokin' hot.

jokes.text: Chris's parting insult: 'I guess I'm not as good a tech as I thought I was. I should have noticed that you're missing a heart.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Chris are saying goodbye after the date ends.
jokes.punchline: Chris frames his MRI incompetence (missing the 'smudge') as actually being real incompetence — but for missing a different problem: Leslie's missing heart.
jokes.explanation: A callback that ties Chris's MRI incompetence to a mild insult. The structure is clean — framing 'no heart' as something an MRI should detect — and Leslie's 'Ew' response is a perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Jean-Ralphio? That idiot once tried to make a margarita in a blender while it was running. He held his hand over the top to see if it was mixing. They had to reattach two of his fingers.

jokes.text: Leslie, after the date, realizing she drove: 'Right. I drove us here. Goodie.'
jokes.setup: Leslie ends the date and turns to leave.
jokes.punchline: She remembers she drove them both — meaning she has to endure more time with Chris — and her defeated 'Goodie' sells the exhaustion perfectly.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly economical button on the date sequence. 'Goodie' does a lot of work — it's sarcastic, defeated, and Leslie-appropriate (she'd normally use 'goodie' sincerely). Great timing.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'll be your assistant. I know you don't want someone who's enthusiastic, or competent, or cares about anything.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I will do the bare minimum, and I will do it with complete indifference.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're hired.

jokes.text: Chris asks if they can pick up his son Nate at a basketball game on the way back.
jokes.setup: Leslie is already stuck driving Chris home after breaking up with him.
jokes.punchline: He asks to add a child pickup to the post-breakup drive — a perfect escalation of the date's absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation of an already disastrous date — Chris adds a whole new dimension of obligation after Leslie has already ended things. A great final beat on his character arc in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I can scare people away.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're hired.

jokes.text: Leslie's date postmortem: 'Well, the good news is, I don't have cancer. The bad news is, I got an MRI bill for $2,000.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Leslie debrief about the date.
jokes.punchline: The good news/bad news framing inverts the expected — 'no cancer' is the upside, '$2,000 bill' is the tragedy.
jokes.explanation: Great callback and payoff to the MRI date. The good news/bad news structure works perfectly, and the specificity of $2,000 (a detail from Chris's original offer) makes it a proper callback. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm ready to get back out there and start dating again. I just need to... work my way back in.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that came out wrong.

jokes.text: Tom's response to Leslie's date story: 'Oh. That sounds hot.' Then: 'Ooh, you slept together?' Leslie: 'What? Not sexually.' Tom: 'God, what's wrong with you, Tom?'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to follow Leslie's date story.
jokes.punchline: Tom mishears 'fit' as a sexual situation; after Leslie corrects him with 'Not sexually,' he self-corrects aloud ('God, what's wrong with you, Tom?') — breaking the fourth wall to address his own awfulness.
jokes.explanation: Tom talking to himself in the third person ('God, what's wrong with you, Tom?') is a great character beat — he knows he's wrong but can't help it. The self-rebuke is funnier than the misunderstanding itself. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: To April, our newest employee. May you find the joy in public service that I have. And may you never have to deal with the... the c-r-a-p that I deal with every day.

jokes.text: Tom sees Justin's shirt and says: 'I have the same one. In an extra small.'
jokes.setup: Tom sees Justin at a party/gathering wearing a shirt.
jokes.punchline: Tom's claim to have the same shirt in 'extra small' is delivered as a normal statement — implying he intentionally buys extra small for the fit, which is very Tom.
jokes.explanation: Quick Tom fashion vanity gag. The 'extra small' detail is the joke — Tom buys clothes intentionally small, which is a specific and believable character quirk.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: April, I'm impressed. You've taken initiative, shown loyalty, and created an effective barrier between me and Jerry. That's exactly the kind of work ethic I look for in an employee.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Thanks, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Keep it up.

jokes.text: Andy to Mark: 'Well, well, well. Look who's bothering who now. Seems like the shoe is in the other foot. And the guy who polishes shoes is now me.'
jokes.setup: Mark approaches Andy at the shoe-shine stand to ask about Justin.
jokes.punchline: Andy mangles 'the shoe is on the other foot' into 'the shoe is in the other foot,' then tries to rescue the metaphor by literally tying it to shoe polishing — which makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: Classic Andy malapropism — 'the shoe is IN the other foot' is a great garbled idiom, and his attempt to connect it to shoe shining doubles down on the confusion. The self-satisfaction in his delivery is key. High character integration: only Andy would mangle an idiom and then try to defend it.

jokes.text: Andy's three-tier ranking system for Ann's loves: 'In terms of guys that she's in love with, Justin's up here, I'm up here, and then you're down here.' (gesturing with hands at different heights)
jokes.setup: Mark asks Andy about Ann's relationship with Justin.
jokes.punchline: Andy helpfully ranks himself and Justin at the same high level, then places Mark significantly lower — apparently not registering this as an insult to the person he's talking to.
jokes.explanation: Great Andy oblivious comedy. He ranks himself and Justin equally (Andy's delusion about his own standing), then casually places Mark much lower — the man he's supposedly helping — without noticing how brutal that is. The physical gesture is implied but essential. High character integration.

jokes.text: Mark's response: 'Well, I just wanted to make sure I wasn't crazy, so, naturally, I came to you for reassurance.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just told Mark he's the least loved person in Ann's life.
jokes.punchline: Mark's wry comment that going to Andy for reassurance was 'natural' — when it clearly wasn't — is a dry self-awareness that he made things worse.
jokes.explanation: Mark's dry delivery of his own foolishness is a good straight-man beat. 'Naturally, I came to you for reassurance' acknowledges the absurdity of consulting his romantic rival for comfort.

jokes.text: Andy's argument to Ann about Justin: 'Every time I used to sit around all afternoon playing video games wearing only my slippers, all of a sudden, I would start to feel bad about myself... I would feel bad about myself because I would start to think about this perfect guy.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to tell Ann what she did wrong (keeping Justin as a backup).
jokes.punchline: His argument begins with a self-portrait so specific and unflattering — 'playing video games wearing only my slippers' — that Ann's voice of reason instinctively responds: 'Didn't you just explain why?'
jokes.explanation: Andy's unintentional self-incrimination is the joke — he describes a lifestyle so depressing that Ann's interruption ('Didn't you just explain why?') perfectly captures the audience's reaction. The specificity ('only my slippers') is key to Andy's oblivious character comedy.

jokes.text: Ann's interruption: 'Didn't you just explain why?' (in response to Andy's self-portrait of playing video games in only slippers)
jokes.setup: Andy is building to a point about why Ann shouldn't emotionally cheat; his setup is a description of his own lazy, depressing lifestyle.
jokes.punchline: Ann cuts through his argument by pointing out he's already explained why she left him.
jokes.explanation: The perfect straight-man callback within a scene. Ann's six-word interruption ('Didn't you just explain why?') is both funny and devastating — it's the most efficient possible response to Andy's unintentional self-condemnation. High economy.

jokes.text: Andy to Ann: 'It's either me or Justin.' Ann: 'I'm not gonna choose.' Andy: 'Wait. I'm dating Mark!' Ann: 'Are you, though?' Andy: 'Yes!' Ann: 'Ah! That close.'
jokes.setup: Andy is giving Ann an ultimatum about Justin.
jokes.punchline: Ann points out she's dating Mark, not Andy; Andy's 'Are you, though?' questions the reality of a relationship that doesn't involve him. His 'That close' (suggesting she nearly chose him) is the delusional button.
jokes.explanation: One of the best exchanges in the episode. Andy giving Ann an ultimatum about a man she's not even dating is already absurd; his 'Are you, though?' genuinely questioning her relationship with Mark is the peak of his delusional confidence. 'Ah! That close.' — suggesting his non-relationship nearly won out — is a perfect button. High character integration, high quotability.

jokes.text: Justin reviews the cease-and-desist letter: 'Check out paragraph two. I drop the F-bomb.' Leslie: 'Frivolous.' Justin: 'Excellent.'
jokes.setup: Justin presents a strongly worded legal letter, warning Leslie she might be frightened by the language.
jokes.punchline: The 'F-bomb' is 'frivolous' — a legal term, not profanity — and Leslie's reading of it ('Frivolous') followed by Justin's 'Excellent' is a perfect payoff.
jokes.explanation: A classically structured misdirection joke. The setup ('I drop the F-bomb') primes the audience for profanity; the reveal ('Frivolous') is both the subversion and a perfect legal detail. The economy is superb — three words deliver the punchline. The structure is near-perfect. One of the episode's best crafted jokes.

jokes.text: Tom to Leslie about Justin: 'Damn! He is all right. Why don't you hit that?'
jokes.setup: Justin has left after delivering the legal letter.
jokes.punchline: Tom's blunt 'Why don't you hit that?' is both a genuine question and Tom's inimitable way of expressing that Leslie should date Justin.
jokes.explanation: A quick Tom character moment, but not deeply crafted. The phrasing is Tom-appropriate but the joke itself is simple. Functions as a transition beat.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Maybe she's got him on hold.' (About Ann 'saving' Justin)
jokes.setup: Leslie explains Ann is being weird about her pursuing Justin.
jokes.punchline: Tom summarizes Ann's emotional reserve-list for Justin as 'having him on hold' — a perfect modern-relationship idiom.
jokes.explanation: Tom's 'on hold' metaphor is a clean, economical bit of modern relationship vocabulary. Brief and functional.

jokes.text: Tom introduces Jean-Ralphio: 'His name is Jean-Ralphio.' Ron: 'Jean-Ralphio!' Jean-Ralphio: 'Big T.'
jokes.setup: Tom promises to find Ron a great assistant.
jokes.punchline: Ron's involuntary exclamation of the name 'Jean-Ralphio!' (apparently in disbelief) is the first joke; Jean-Ralphio's immediate nickname for Tom ('Big T') signals his personality immediately.
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's introduction is a character comedy masterclass in economy — Ron's incredulous exclamation and Jean-Ralphio's immediate 'Big T' establish everything you need to know about both characters in two words each.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio to Ron: 'Mr. Swanson, two things. One, it is an absolute honor to meet you. Two, who is that hot intern chick out there? Because honestly, damn!'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is meeting Ron Swanson for the first time in a job interview.
jokes.punchline: He pivots from flattering Ron to immediately objectifying a woman in the office — 'Because honestly, damn!' — in the span of one breath, showing his complete lack of professional awareness.
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's oblivious swagger is captured perfectly in this intro — the pivot from professional greeting to leering is instant and complete. The 'honestly, damn!' is a great character note delivered with total confidence.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio's pitch to Ron: 'For starters, access to the illest clubs... I'll be on you 24/7. I'll be like your family. I'm here when you get here in the morning. Sure enough, I'll be there tucking you into bed at night. Don't worry, it's not gay.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is selling himself as Ron's assistant.
jokes.punchline: His pitch escalates from nightclub access to 24/7 presence to literally tucking Ron into bed, then adds 'Don't worry, it's not gay' — a preemptive disclaimer that makes everything more alarming.
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's escalating pitch is a great character comedy escalation. 'Tucking you into bed' followed by 'Don't worry, it's not gay' is a perfect absurdist button — the disclaimer makes the whole thing more inappropriate, not less. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Ron immediately says 'I think our only question is when can you start?' Then when Jean-Ralphio leaves, tells Tom: 'I want to punch you in the face so bad right now.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio gives his pitch; Ron's response appears to be enthusiastic approval ('When can you start?').
jokes.punchline: The moment Jean-Ralphio leaves, Ron reveals he hated the interview and wants to punch Tom. The politeness was a mask.
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection followed by a perfectly Ron line. 'I want to punch you in the face so bad right now' is quintessential Ron — contained fury expressed with complete directness. The structure (fake enthusiasm → suppressed rage) is expertly executed. High quotability.

jokes.text: Ron's instruction to Tom after the Jean-Ralphio interview: 'Bring me the opposite of him.'
jokes.setup: Tom asks what Ron thought of Jean-Ralphio.
jokes.punchline: 'Bring me the opposite of him' is the most efficient possible way to reject someone without specific criticism — Ron can't even articulate what was wrong, he just wants the inverse.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Five words, perfect economy, completely in character. 'Bring me the opposite of him' captures Ron's disdain without elaboration, which is exactly Ron. The economy score is 10 — you cannot say this with fewer words. High quotability. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor and above.

jokes.text: Andy selling his band's CD to a customer: '[describing his music] The kind that sticks in your brain. Loud, fast, smooth, handsome rock.' Customer: 'That band is really blowing up right now. They're number one on iTunes.' Andy: 'Okay. I'll take one.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to sell a CD of his own band's music at the shoe-shine stand.
jokes.punchline: The customer's claim that the band is 'number one on iTunes' — presumably untrue or referring to something else — leads Andy to buy his own CD, apparently not recognizing it's his band.
jokes.explanation: Great Andy moment — he's so susceptible to flattery that he buys his own music because someone says it's popular. The description 'smooth, handsome rock' is also a good character beat. High character integration.

jokes.text: April asks to be Ron's assistant: 'So do you. I'll make sure you don't have to go to any meetings. If anyone comes to see you, I'll scare them away.'
jokes.setup: April says she wants to be Ron's assistant because she hates working there.
jokes.punchline: Her pitch is exactly what Ron wants — protecting him from meetings and public contact — and it's also completely inappropriate as a job description.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully crafted character comedy pairing. April's pitch — protecting Ron from his own job — is the exact opposite of a job description, but it's precisely what Ron wants. The two characters are perfectly matched here. 'I'll scare them away' is a great April line. High character integration for both characters.

jokes.text: Ron's tie test for April: she immediately picks the correct one. Ron: 'You're hired.'
jokes.setup: Ron asks April which tie he should wear — the same test he uses for all assistant candidates.
jokes.punchline: April picks correctly (or Ron simply trusts her taste), and he hires her on the spot — a callback to the elaborate tie test that failed every other candidate.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback — the test that eliminated all of Tom's candidates works instantly with April. Ron's immediate 'You're hired' is perfectly economical. The structural payoff (two characters who hate their jobs finding each other) earns the laugh.

jokes.text: April: 'I just figured I might as well get paid for being here.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just hired April as his assistant.
jokes.punchline: April's reason for wanting the job is pure nihilistic pragmatism — she's here anyway, she might as well monetize it.
jokes.explanation: Perfect April line — her motivation for a promotion is not ambition but pure logistical convenience. 'I might as well get paid for being here' is deeply in character and delivered with exactly the right amount of boredom. High economy and character integration.

jokes.text: April's talking-head: 'I just figured I might as well get paid for being here.'
jokes.setup: April has just become Ron's official assistant.
jokes.punchline: Her motivation for taking the job is pure pragmatic laziness — she was going to be there doing nothing anyway.
jokes.explanation: Perfect April. The deadpan logic — 'I'm here anyway, might as well monetize my presence' — is completely consistent with her character and delivered with zero enthusiasm. Economy score is near-max.

jokes.text: Ann gives Leslie a prescription meant for 'Denise Dogan' by mistake.
jokes.setup: Ann rushes to find Leslie to tell her about Justin.
jokes.punchline: In her distraction, Ann gives Leslie a prescription intended for a patient — a casual HIPAA violation that she doesn't notice.
jokes.explanation: Quick visual gag — Ann accidentally delivering a patient's prescription to Leslie is a nice nurse character moment. Brief and functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Ann to Mark: 'I rented District 9 if you maybe wanted to spoil that for me tonight.'
jokes.setup: Ann is apologizing to Mark for the Justin situation and trying to make it up to him.
jokes.punchline: Her peace offering is letting Mark spoil District 9 for her — framing it as a gift to him, which is an odd kind of intimacy.
jokes.explanation: A charming and specific relationship joke — 'letting' someone spoil a movie for you as a gesture of affection. The specificity of District 9 is a nice period touch.

jokes.text: Mark immediately spoils District 9: 'Dark ending, right?' Ann: 'Oh, my God!'
jokes.setup: Ann has offered to let Mark spoil District 9.
jokes.punchline: Mark instantly spoils it with 'Dark ending, right?' — a callback that pays off the joke immediately and gets an exasperated reaction from Ann.
jokes.explanation: The immediate payoff is the joke — Ann barely finishes offering the gift before Mark unwraps it. 'Dark ending, right?' is a perfectly timed three-word spoiler. Ann's 'Oh, my God!' sells it. A great tight callback.

jokes.text: Leslie in talking head: 'I'm back on the horse, and this horse is a lawyer, so I'm looking forward to riding him. No, wait.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is expressing optimism about her upcoming date with Justin.
jokes.punchline: She uses the 'back on the horse' metaphor but extends it to include 'riding him' — immediately catching the sexual implication and trying to walk it back with 'No, wait.'
jokes.explanation: A classic unintentional double entendre followed by Leslie's dawning horror. The 'No, wait' is perfectly Leslie — she's not trying to make the joke, which is what makes it work. Good structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head: 'I'm back on the horse, and this horse is a lawyer, so I'm looking forward to riding him. No, wait.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has a date set up with Justin.
jokes.punchline: Leslie realizes mid-metaphor that 'riding the lawyer-horse' sounds sexual and immediately corrects herself — but the pause before 'No, wait' implies she knows exactly what she said.
jokes.explanation: A well-timed confessional joke. The setup ('back on the horse') is a common idiom; Leslie's literal extension of it into 'this horse is a lawyer' is funny, and then the dawning horror of 'riding him' followed by 'No, wait' is a perfect talking-head comedy beat. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Ron's announcement: 'Ten months ago, she was an intern who could give a C-R-A-P about local government. Now she's our newest employee. To April!'
jokes.setup: Ron is making a toast to celebrate April becoming a permanent employee.
jokes.punchline: Ron's toast is a backhanded praise — 'could give a C-R-A-P' (spelling it out, weirdly formally) — which is actually an anti-endorsement that he somehow frames as a celebration.
jokes.explanation: Ron spelling out 'C-R-A-P' in a formal toast is a great oddity — why spell it? — and the substance of his toast is essentially praise for not caring. Very Ron. High character integration.

jokes.text: Jerry tries to talk to Ron directly after being told to schedule an appointment. April blocks him: 'Ron's not here.' Jerry: 'He's right there. I can see him.' April: 'I'll let you know when he's available.'
jokes.setup: Jerry wants to talk to Ron about his desk size.
jokes.punchline: April, now Ron's assistant, denies Ron's presence despite Jerry clearly seeing him — her new job's first act is lying about Ron's visibility with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: A perfect payoff to April's hiring. Her first act as assistant is exactly what she promised: blocking Ron from visitors through brazen denial of reality. 'He's right there. I can see him.' / 'I'll let you know when he's available' is a great exchange. High character integration for both April and Ron.

jokes.text: Ron's reaction to April stonewalling Jerry: 'Attagirl.'
jokes.setup: April has just denied Ron's existence to Jerry while Ron watches.
jokes.punchline: Ron's single-word approval — 'Attagirl' — is the ultimate validation of both April's performance and Ron's worldview.
jokes.explanation: The perfect episode button. One word — 'Attagirl' — delivers Ron's complete endorsement of April's obstruction. It's the payoff to the entire assistant subplot: Ron found someone who hates the public as much as he does. Economy is a 10. Character integration is a 10. This is the kind of line that becomes iconic for a character. One of the episode's top moments.

tmdb_overview: Ann sets Leslie up on a blind date with a co-worker, which does not go as well as Leslie hoped. An old friend of Ann's makes Mark feel insecure.
insight: Romantic subplot undercuts comedy momentum; character humor drops below season average.
